lesson.title: Equations' Flexible Cousin: What Makes an Inequality Linear
lesson.summary: Recognize the standard form of a linear inequality in one variable and see how it compares to a linear equation, setting up the solving techniques covered later in this unit.
lesson.body:
A linear inequality looks almost exactly like a linear equation in one variable, with one important difference: somewhere in place of the equals sign sits an inequality symbol, such as less than, greater than, less than or equal to, or greater than or equal to. Just as a linear equation in one variable can be written in the form ax plus b equals c, where the variable x appears only to the first power and is never multiplied by itself or placed under a root or in a denominator, a linear inequality has the same restriction on the variable, written instead as ax plus b is less than c, or with any of the other three inequality symbols in place of less than.

This shared structure is exactly why linear inequalities can borrow so much from what you already know about linear equations. Expressions like 3x plus 7, or 2 times the quantity x minus 4, simplify the same way whether they sit next to an equals sign or an inequality symbol, using the distributive property and combining like terms exactly as before. What changes is not how the expressions themselves are simplified, but how the final answer is interpreted and, as the next section covers in detail, one extra rule that applies only when both sides are multiplied or divided by a negative number.

For now, focus on recognizing the form and reading it correctly. The statement 3x minus 4 is less than 11 is a linear inequality in one variable, because x appears only to the first power. By contrast, x squared is less than 11 is not a linear inequality, since squaring the variable takes it out of linear form entirely, and belongs to a different family of inequalities covered in a later course. A statement like 3x minus 4 equals 11, with an equals sign instead of an inequality symbol, is a linear equation, not a linear inequality, even though the left side looks identical.

Consider the linear inequality 3x minus 4 is less than 11. Testing a specific value shows what a solution looks like: substituting x equals 0 gives 3 times 0 minus 4, which is negative 4, and negative 4 is indeed less than 11, so x equals 0 is one solution among many. Testing the boundary value x equals 5 gives 3 times 5 minus 4, which is 11, and since 11 is not less than 11, x equals 5 is not a solution, even though it is very close to the boundary of the solution set. This idea, that a linear inequality has a whole boundary line between the numbers that work and the numbers that do not, is the foundation for solving these inequalities systematically and for graphing their solutions on a number line in the sections that follow.

It also helps to notice that a linear inequality can be written with the variable on either side of the inequality symbol, just as a linear equation can. The statement 11 is greater than 3x minus 4 describes exactly the same relationship as 3x minus 4 is less than 11, simply read in the opposite direction, in the same way that a equals b and b equals a describe the same equation. Some students find it easier to rearrange an inequality so the variable sits on the left before solving it, and that rearrangement is always valid as long as the direction of the symbol is flipped to match, a small preview of the more important flipping rule covered when negative numbers enter the picture in the next section on solving linear inequalities.
